content: Trench fever is an infectious disease characterized by intermittent episodes of fever, chills, and splenomegaly, with each episode potentially lasting up to 40 hours. The causative agent is Bartonella quintana, which is transmitted to humans via the human body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis). Historically, the disease was prevalent among soldiers during World War I and World War II, with significant outbreaks reported among British, German, and Austrian troops. Between 1915 and 1918, trench fever accounted for illness in approximately one-fifth to one-third of British troops and one-fifth of German and Austrian troops. The pathophysiology of trench fever involves the transmission of Bartonella quintana through contamination of skin abrasions or louse-bite wounds with the feces of infected body lice. There have also been reports of direct transmission through the bite of an infected louse. The organism resides in the stomach walls of the body louse and is closely related to other pathogenic microbes, such as those causing Rocky Mountain spotted fever and typhus. Epidemiologically, outbreaks of trench fever have been documented in various locations, including Seattle, Washington, and Baltimore, Maryland, in the United States, particularly among injection drug users. Other outbreaks have occurred in Marseille, France, and Burundi. The natural history of the disease is generally non-lethal, but in rare cases, persistent fever can lead to complications such as heart failure. Long-term sequelae may include neurasthenia, cardiac disturbances, and myalgia. The clinical presentation of trench fever typically involves a relapsing five-day fever, although continuous fever is occasionally observed. The incubation period is relatively long, averaging about two weeks. Symptoms often begin suddenly and include high fever, severe headache, pain with eye movement, muscle soreness in the legs and back, and hypersensitivity of the shins. The most consistent symptom is leg pain. Recovery can take a month or longer. Diagnosis is often confirmed through serological testing, such as the Weil-Felix test, although these tests are typically effective only after a week or more following symptom onset. Treatment primarily involves antibiotics from the tetracycline group, such as doxycycline or tetracycline, administered for seven to ten days. Chloramphenicol is an alternative treatment option for patients in whom tetracycline derivatives are contraindicated, such as those with severe liver or kidney dysfunction, children under nine years of age, or pregnant women. For bacillary angiomatosis, a related condition, erythromycin is the recommended treatment, typically given for three to four months.
